identity.name: FINEOTEX CHEMICAL LIMITED

summary.oneLiner: The CrudeChem acquisition has stopped being an integration story and become the company: total income tripled to ₹386.72cr (+165% YoY), oil & gas is now **65% of revenue** (~₹250cr) against a flat-to-slightly-down textile base (₹132cr vs ₹137cr), and consolidated EBITDA margin has climbed back from a post-deal trough of ~14% to **15.70%** as US operating efficiency, supplier renegotiation and green-chemistry mix all landed together. Texas capacity was nearly doubled to 148,000 MTPA during the quarter and is already running at 63% on a **single shift** — so management's USD 100mn (FY27) / USD 200mn (FY28) oil & gas revenue guide needs almost no further capital, only USD 1-2mn for a second shift. The risk is that the whole thesis now rests on one 53%-owned US subsidiary in a cyclical end-market, with no order book in the conventional sense.

> **Distortions to call out:** (a) The **standalone** entity shows a marginal revenue/EBITDA *decline*, which is purely optical — new product lines have shifted to **FSPL Specialties**, the wholly-owned Indian subsidiary housing the plant commissioned in August 2025 under the 15% Sec-115BAB regime. Indian operations must be read as FCL standalone **plus** FSPL; combined, there is no dip. (b) PAT growth (+93%) trails EBITDA growth (+135%) because FCL owns only 53% of CCTL while consolidating 100% of its revenue under Ind AS — the 47% minority interest sits below the line. (c) Textile revenue of ~₹132cr vs ₹137cr is described as "1% or 2% plus-minus", attributed to monsoon seasonality and a mix shift away from expensive performance chemicals, not demand loss. (d) Forex on the US business is disclosed as a separate foreign-exchange line, not inside other income; CCTL buys and sells in dollars, giving a natural hedge alongside FCL's dollar raw-material imports.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Oil & gas / CrudeChem revenue: USD 100mn in FY27 and USD 200mn in FY28** — reaffirmed. Management explicitly de-linked this from crude prices: "*It is not related to the crude oil prices at all*", arguing extraction economics (Middle East lifting cost <$10, US <$30) and multi-year production commitments mean activity does not stop at $60 crude. Timing framed as "*by 2028 December, you will be happy… I think we should be achieving it*", with an escape clause: "*If it is not achieved as soon as possible, it will be achieved in a little bit more extra time.*"
- **Consolidated EBITDA margin: 18%** — the previously stated target, confirmed on the call when an analyst framed it as "the margin trajectory that you have predicted to 18%" ("*Yes, yes*"). But management simultaneously **refuses to run the business to a margin number**: "*we cannot have any fixed blended margins ever… we do not go for a clear-cut guidance that this was the EBITDA percentage, otherwise we are not taking the business ahead.*" Treat 18% as an aspiration with a stated willingness to trade it for volume and customer engagement.
- **Texas capacity utilisation: full utilisation "in the coming few quarters"** — from 63% today on one shift, with "*we can easily add another 30%, 40% on that business itself.*"
- **Q1 FY27 as the floor:** "*this should be one of our base quarter going forward in terms of capacity utilizations and also the maximum revenue what we can get out of this*" — management explicitly nominated this quarter (consolidated) as the base to compound off.
- **Incremental capex for the next leg: USD 1-2mn only**, to run a second shift — "*it's not going to be more than USD 2 million or USD 1 million… not going to change the world for Fineotex.*"
- **Margins sustainable through the war/price cycle:** raw-material moves are passed on in both directions while preserving absolute margin per gallon/pound, supported by the US market's accepted "war surcharge" / fuel-surcharge mechanism levied on customers and by suppliers on FCL.
- **Textile:** no numeric guide. Management called it "*on auto run*" and expects improvement in coming quarters on the back of UK/EU/US trade normalisation, an expanded Bangladesh marketing/technical team, Bharat Tex leads and further international exhibitions.
- **M&A:** actively evaluating; criteria are (1) synergy and (2) value; will disclose to exchanges when advanced. No segment or timeline committed.
order book & pipeline: **Management explicitly rejects the order-book construct for the US oilfield business:** "*in terms of general order book, there is nothing as such like order book… it's not a government order or tender.*" Demand comes in bunches tied to well activity, interrupted by weather (storms, snowfall), but is described as "*perennial*" because once a well is in production it cannot be stopped. Forward pipeline evidence given instead: Canada sales commenced last month; Suriname and Guyana identified as hard-core oil-producing geographies where service operators are asking FCL to set up local production; a Saudi order won after two years of R&D, where **a customer of FCL's has won a USD 8bn Aramco order requiring FCL's specialty package**. Customer set is the top four or five global service operators plus majors (ExxonMobil, Halliburton, Chevron, ConocoPhillips referenced as examples of the class, not as a disclosed list).
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Oil & gas (CrudeChem/CCTL, 53% owned, USA):** ~65% of revenue (~₹250cr), ~55% of volume. Texas plant expanded by 69,000 MTPA to 148,000 MTPA during the quarter, plus the strategically located Midland facility. Implied standalone EBITDA margin "*minimum 13%, 13% to 14%*". Improvements attributed to technology transfer from India, cross-selling, better supplier pricing enabled by FCL's capital infusion, and a growing green-chemistry mix that carries better profitability. Also runs **Trackmax**, a separately incorporated last-mile delivery and telematics business — deliberately ring-fenced because US auto/workmen/driver insurance and litigation risk should not sit inside CCTL. Management is emphatic that last-mile delivery is a *margin source*, not a cost: US customers "*are ready to pay you more price as long as you do the services.*"
- **Textile specialty chemicals (India + Malaysia + exports):** ~₹132cr vs ₹137cr YoY — flat. Monsoon seasonality plus a trend shift away from expensive performance chemicals. Historically 95% of the business from 2011 to ~2022-23 with a >30% CAGR over that period. Team expanded in Bangladesh; participating in Bharat Tex and further international textile exhibitions.
- **FSPL Specialties (100% Indian subsidiary):** new plant commissioned August 2025, taxed at 15% under Sec 115BAB; now carries several new product lines — the reason FCL standalone shows an optical dip.
- **Malaysian subsidiary (72%, acquired 2011):** confirmed to be improving alongside the other entities.
- Products sold across **more than 70 countries**.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Geographic expansion of the oilfield business:** Canada live from last month; Suriname and Guyana where service operators are actively soliciting local production capability; Saudi Arabia newly won after a two-year R&D cycle.
- **Green chemistry / sustainable oilfield solutions** — repeatedly named as the structural tailwind and the higher-margin end of the portfolio, with majors and service operators all pursuing sustainability mandates. FCL cites a Dun & Bradstreet ESG badge as a commercial door-opener.
- **Cross-selling and Asia sourcing:** offering CCTL's US customers product made in India or Malaysia.
- **Technical textiles** — automotive, medical, industrial, infrastructure applications flagged as long-term optionality within the textile business.
- **M&A** — this would be the third acquisition (Malaysia 2011, CrudeChem 2025), with a dedicated M&A head (Yusuf Contractor) hired from a large global specialty chemicals player.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Growth capital as the acquisition thesis, evidenced by the outcome.** Management describes CrudeChem not as a bolt-on but as a business that needed capital to scale: "*we have given the growth capital to CrudeChem, that's why you can see flying colors from the time we have entered*" — and notes that **CrudeChem's own customers advised it to tie up with Fineotex**. The capital infusion also unlocked better supplier pricing, feeding directly into EBITDA.
- **Last-mile delivery as a structural US advantage.** Owning the delivery fleet (via Trackmax) rather than outsourcing is why CrudeChem earns a better margin and is preferred by USD 100bn+ customers who need door delivery, full insurance and reliability — and are willing to pay for it because the chemical is a small share of their cost. Explicitly contrasted with Indian buyer behaviour.
- **Cost position versus US specialty chemical incumbents:** "*we are competing with the USA top specialty chemical companies and because of we being more leaner, we have an edge on pricing and the performance is equivalent.*"
- **Contractual pass-through in both directions.** Raw-material moves are passed through while preserving absolute margin per gallon/pound, and the US market's accepted "war surcharge" mechanism makes freight/geopolitical cost recoverable — the model is explicitly *not* a trading/inventory-gain model.
- **Non-capex-intensive specialty economics.** ROIC 33%, ROCE 25.6% across 60 quarters as a listed company, sustained because the company deliberately selects high-gross-margin, solution-based product lines rather than commodity volume.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin rose to 35.42% (from ~29-30% in Q4FY26 and ~33% a year ago) on successful pass-through of Middle-East-driven raw-material inflation. EBITDA margin 15.70%, up ~150bps QoQ from 13.93%; implied CCTL standalone EBITDA margin 13-14%, which management calls "*very good in terms of these volumes*". Drivers of the US margin expansion: technology transfer and product modification from India, cross-selling, a richer green-chemistry mix, and — most concretely — **better supplier pricing negotiated on the back of FCL's capital infusion**. The 18% consolidated target is acknowledged but explicitly subordinated to winning volume and long-term customer contracts. Cost recovery on freight/geopolitics runs through a formal US surcharge mechanism levied on customers (and by FCL's suppliers on FCL), which management treats as effectively a reimbursement. Management refused to quantify current-versus-pre-war chemical price levels, noting the "pre-war price" framing itself collapsed within a week — "*war is still going on, it just took an interval… It's the new normal.*"
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **Texas expansion commissioned during the quarter**: +69,000 MTPA taking the plant to 148,000 MTPA (group ~268,000 MTPA) — *already done*, not a forward promise. Includes new machinery capable of higher-performance product lines, not merely replicated reactors.
- **Running at 63% on a single shift** — the next tranche of growth comes from a second shift, requiring only **USD 1-2mn**. This is the single most important structural point on the call: the USD 100mn→USD 200mn revenue path is largely capex-free.
- FSPL Specialties plant (India) commissioned August 2025, now absorbing new product lines under a 15% tax regime.
- Possible local production set-up in Suriname/Guyana at customer request — no commitment, no number.
capital allocation: Self-described as cash-disciplined with "very high cash on book" and a 72-day working capital cycle. Two acquisitions in 15 listed years (Malaysia 2011 with IPO proceeds; CrudeChem December 2025), with stated screens of synergy plus value for shareholders. Capital is currently going into: US capacity (done), the FSPL India plant (done), R&D and doctorate-level hiring in the USA, and working-capital extension plus raw-material procurement support for CCTL. Further inorganic activity is under active discussion with a dedicated M&A head, to be disclosed to exchanges when advanced. No dividend or buyback discussion on this call.
risks & watch-items:
- **Concentration into one 53%-owned US subsidiary.** Two-thirds of revenue now comes from CCTL, in which FCL consolidates 100% of revenue but owns 53% — visible as the gap between EBITDA growth (+135%) and PAT growth (+93%). An analyst tried twice to pin down the minority-interest arithmetic and was deferred offline.
- **No order book, by management's own description.** The USD 100mn/USD 200mn guide rests on well activity, customer relationships and a "perennial" production assumption — not on contracted backlog. Weather alone stops work for one to two weeks at a time.
- **The crude-independence claim is untested at low prices.** Management asserts activity is insensitive to crude down to $60 or below on lifting-cost logic, while simultaneously conceding "*the higher the crude oil prices, the activity in U.S. is always higher.*" Crude was cited around $90-100 at the time of the call — the assertion has not yet been stress-tested.
- **Margin guidance is explicitly non-binding.** The 18% target coexists with a stated policy of never turning away business on margin grounds. Do not treat 18% as a hard commitment.
- **Textile is flat and has been for a year** — ~₹132cr vs ₹137cr, with the recovery case resting on UK/EU/US trade normalisation, exhibition leads and Bangladesh team expansion. No number was offered for the base business over two-to-three years despite a direct request.
- **Guidance slipped its own frame mid-answer.** The FY28 USD 200mn target was restated as "by 2028 December" — a calendar-year framing that does not match FY28, followed by an explicit allowance for "a little bit more extra time." Worth nailing down next quarter.
- **Disclosure granularity.** CCTL standalone margins had to be back-solved from the blend; CCTL order book was declined; the forex accounting question was deflected as immaterial ("*I don't know how important is this question*"). Several answers were long, discursive and hard to pin to numbers.
- **Litigation/insurance exposure in the US** is real enough that logistics had to be incorporated separately ("*in US, it's very common to sue each other*").
management quality / tone: Energetic and commercially specific where it matters — the capacity, utilisation, shift-economics and supplier-negotiation answers were concrete and internally consistent, and the CFO was refreshingly direct that a USD 1-2mn capex question "*is not going to be a topic of discussion*" when the real variable is winning share at the majors. Candour is high on structure (the FSPL optical-dip explanation, the deliberate ring-fencing of Trackmax, the CrudeChem minority arithmetic) and lower on precision (CCTL margins, forex treatment and the exact FY28 timing were all softened or deferred). The refusal to commit to a fixed blended EBITDA margin is intellectually honest for a 100+ SKU solutions business, but it does hollow out the 18% target that analysts keep anchoring to. Notably, management chose to disclose a customer's USD 8bn Aramco win as evidence of its own specialty package qualifying — a second-hand proof point, but a checkable one.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The next doubling of the US business is essentially free.** Texas is at 63% utilisation **on one shift**; a second shift costs USD 1-2mn. The USD 100mn→USD 200mn revenue path therefore requires almost no incremental capital, which is why ROCE/ROIC should hold or improve as revenue scales — a very different capital-intensity profile from most chemicals expansions.
- **The standalone "decline" is an artefact of tax structuring.** New product lines were deliberately housed in FSPL Specialties to access the 15% Sec-115BAB rate; Indian operations must be read as FCL standalone plus FSPL. Anyone screening on standalone numbers will misread the India business.
- **Last-mile logistics is a margin business, not a cost centre** — and it is incorporated separately purely to keep US insurance and litigation exposure out of the operating entity. Both halves of that are unusual and both are deliberate.
- **The "war surcharge" is an institutionalised US market mechanism**, levied by FCL on customers and by FCL's suppliers on FCL — which is why geopolitical cost shocks are largely margin-neutral here, unlike for Indian-domiciled chemical exporters.
- **CrudeChem's own customers pushed it toward Fineotex.** Management says service operators advised the target to take growth capital from FCL — a validation of counterparty credibility that is more meaningful than the deal multiple.
- **A second-order revenue proof point:** an FCL customer won a USD 8bn Aramco contract requiring FCL's specialty package, after two years of R&D spend. This is the concrete evidence behind the Middle East expansion claim.

- **Green chemistry / sustainable oilfield solutions** — repeatedly named as the structural tailwind and the higher-margin end of the portfolio, with majors and service operators all pursuing sustainability mandates. FCL cites a Dun & Bradstreet ESG badge as a commercial door-opener.
- **Cross-selling and Asia sourcing:** offering CCTL's US customers product made in India or Malaysia.
- **Technical textiles** — automotive, medical, industrial, infrastructure applications flagged as long-term optionality within the textile business.
- **M&A** — this would be the third acquisition (Malaysia 2011, CrudeChem 2025), with a dedicated M&A head (Yusuf Contractor) hired from a large global specialty chemicals player.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Growth capital as the acquisition thesis, evidenced by the outcome.** Management describes CrudeChem not as a bolt-on but as a business that needed capital to scale: "*we have given the growth capital to CrudeChem, that's why you can see flying colors from the time we have entered*" — and notes that **CrudeChem's own customers advised it to tie up with Fineotex**. The capital infusion also unlocked better supplier pricing, feeding directly into EBITDA.
- **Last-mile delivery as a structural US advantage.** Owning the delivery fleet (via Trackmax) rather than outsourcing is why CrudeChem earns a better margin and is preferred by USD 100bn+ customers who need door delivery, full insurance and reliability — and are willing to pay for it because the chemical is a small share of their cost. Explicitly contrasted with Indian buyer behaviour.
- **Cost position versus US specialty chemical incumbents:** "*we are competing with the USA top specialty chemical companies and because of we being more leaner, we have an edge on pricing and the performance is equivalent.*"
- **Contractual pass-through in both directions.** Raw-material moves are passed through while preserving absolute margin per gallon/pound, and the US market's accepted "war surcharge" mechanism makes freight/geopolitical cost recoverable — the model is explicitly *not* a trading/inventory-gain model.
- **Non-capex-intensive specialty economics.** ROIC 33%, ROCE 25.6% across 60 quarters as a listed company, sustained because the company deliberately selects high-gross-margin, solution-based product lines rather than commodity volume.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin rose to 35.42% (from ~29-30% in Q4FY26 and ~33% a year ago) on successful pass-through of Middle-East-driven raw-material inflation. EBITDA margin 15.70%, up ~150bps QoQ from 13.93%; implied CCTL standalone EBITDA margin 13-14%, which management calls "*very good in terms of these volumes*". Drivers of the US margin expansion: technology transfer and product modification from India, cross-selling, a richer green-chemistry mix, and — most concretely — **better supplier pricing negotiated on the back of FCL's capital infusion**. The 18% consolidated target is acknowledged but explicitly subordinated to winning volume and long-term customer contracts. Cost recovery on freight/geopolitics runs through a formal US surcharge mechanism levied on customers (and by FCL's suppliers on FCL), which management treats as effectively a reimbursement. Management refused to quantify current-versus-pre-war chemical price levels, noting the "pre-war price" framing itself collapsed within a week — "*war is still going on, it just took an interval… It's the new normal.*"
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **Texas expansion commissioned during the quarter**: +69,000 MTPA taking the plant to 148,000 MTPA (group ~268,000 MTPA) — *already done*, not a forward promise. Includes new machinery capable of higher-performance product lines, not merely replicated reactors.
- **Running at 63% on a single shift** — the next tranche of growth comes from a second shift, requiring only **USD 1-2mn**. This is the single most important structural point on the call: the USD 100mn→USD 200mn revenue path is largely capex-free.
- FSPL Specialties plant (India) commissioned August 2025, now absorbing new product lines under a 15% tax regime.
- Possible local production set-up in Suriname/Guyana at customer request — no commitment, no number.
capital allocation: Self-described as cash-disciplined with "very high cash on book" and a 72-day working capital cycle. Two acquisitions in 15 listed years (Malaysia 2011 with IPO proceeds; CrudeChem December 2025), with stated screens of synergy plus value for shareholders. Capital is currently going into: US capacity (done), the FSPL India plant (done), R&D and doctorate-level hiring in the USA, and working-capital extension plus raw-material procurement support for CCTL. Further inorganic activity is under active discussion with a dedicated M&A head, to be disclosed to exchanges when advanced. No dividend or buyback discussion on this call.
risks & watch-items:
- **Concentration into one 53%-owned US subsidiary.** Two-thirds of revenue now comes from CCTL, in which FCL consolidates 100% of revenue but owns 53% — visible as the gap between EBITDA growth (+135%) and PAT growth (+93%). An analyst tried twice to pin down the minority-interest arithmetic and was deferred offline.
- **No order book, by management's own description.** The USD 100mn/USD 200mn guide rests on well activity, customer relationships and a "perennial" production assumption — not on contracted backlog. Weather alone stops work for one to two weeks at a time.
- **The crude-independence claim is untested at low prices.** Management asserts activity is insensitive to crude down to $60 or below on lifting-cost logic, while simultaneously conceding "*the higher the crude oil prices, the activity in U.S. is always higher.*" Crude was cited around $90-100 at the time of the call — the assertion has not yet been stress-tested.
- **Margin guidance is explicitly non-binding.** The 18% target coexists with a stated policy of never turning away business on margin grounds. Do not treat 18% as a hard commitment.
- **Textile is flat and has been for a year** — ~₹132cr vs ₹137cr, with the recovery case resting on UK/EU/US trade normalisation, exhibition leads and Bangladesh team expansion. No number was offered for the base business over two-to-three years despite a direct request.
- **Guidance slipped its own frame mid-answer.** The FY28 USD 200mn target was restated as "by 2028 December" — a calendar-year framing that does not match FY28, followed by an explicit allowance for "a little bit more extra time." Worth nailing down next quarter.
- **Disclosure granularity.** CCTL standalone margins had to be back-solved from the blend; CCTL order book was declined; the forex accounting question was deflected as immaterial ("*I don't know how important is this question*"). Several answers were long, discursive and hard to pin to numbers.
- **Litigation/insurance exposure in the US** is real enough that logistics had to be incorporated separately ("*in US, it's very common to sue each other*").
management quality / tone: Energetic and commercially specific where it matters — the capacity, utilisation, shift-economics and supplier-negotiation answers were concrete and internally consistent, and the CFO was refreshingly direct that a USD 1-2mn capex question "*is not going to be a topic of discussion*" when the real variable is winning share at the majors. Candour is high on structure (the FSPL optical-dip explanation, the deliberate ring-fencing of Trackmax, the CrudeChem minority arithmetic) and lower on precision (CCTL margins, forex treatment and the exact FY28 timing were all softened or deferred). The refusal to commit to a fixed blended EBITDA margin is intellectually honest for a 100+ SKU solutions business, but it does hollow out the 18% target that analysts keep anchoring to. Notably, management chose to disclose a customer's USD 8bn Aramco win as evidence of its own specialty package qualifying — a second-hand proof point, but a checkable one.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The next doubling of the US business is essentially free.** Texas is at 63% utilisation **on one shift**; a second shift costs USD 1-2mn. The USD 100mn→USD 200mn revenue path therefore requires almost no incremental capital, which is why ROCE/ROIC should hold or improve as revenue scales — a very different capital-intensity profile from most chemicals expansions.
- **The standalone "decline" is an artefact of tax structuring.** New product lines were deliberately housed in FSPL Specialties to access the 15% Sec-115BAB rate; Indian operations must be read as FCL standalone plus FSPL. Anyone screening on standalone numbers will misread the India business.
- **Last-mile logistics is a margin business, not a cost centre** — and it is incorporated separately purely to keep US insurance and litigation exposure out of the operating entity. Both halves of that are unusual and both are deliberate.
- **The "war surcharge" is an institutionalised US market mechanism**, levied by FCL on customers and by FCL's suppliers on FCL — which is why geopolitical cost shocks are largely margin-neutral here, unlike for Indian-domiciled chemical exporters.
- **CrudeChem's own customers pushed it toward Fineotex.** Management says service operators advised the target to take growth capital from FCL — a validation of counterparty credibility that is more meaningful than the deal multiple.
- **A second-order revenue proof point:** an FCL customer won a USD 8bn Aramco contract requiring FCL's specialty package, after two years of R&D spend. This is the concrete evidence behind the Middle East expansion claim.

themes.title: Oil & Gas - gas economy (CGD/LNG) + refining/upstream
themes.need: India's gas-economy push now collides with an outright policy reversal. ATGL grew volume 13% to 303 MMSCM and revenue 27% to INR 1,908cr, yet EBITDA FELL sequentially to INR 281cr (~14.7% margin, from INR 310cr) because the government withdrew the pooled-gas mechanism after the West Asia 'peace deal', pushing ATGL to ~15% spot volumes with Brent above $107/bbl; management also noted NWG price is 12% of the Indian crude basket, so a 62% domestic mix protects far less than it looks, and CNG station adds slowed to +5 from +25 in Q4 even as CNG demand grows ~30%. The same shock ran the other way for integrated refining: RELIANCE delivered O2C EBITDA of INR 17,000cr (+17%) THROUGH the Strait-of-Hormuz closure at 96-97% throughput while Asian peers ran 15-20% below capacity, with ethane+ROGC at ~70% of ethylene feed as distillate cracks blew out (gas oil $16 to $63, ATF $14 to $62). MGL/GUJGASLTD/IGL/IRMENERGY carry the same CGD margin squeeze; PETRONET/OIL/ONGC/IOC ride LNG-infra + domestic-gas; CHENNPETRO/MRPL ride GRM cracks; DEEPINDS/JINDRILL/SEAMECLTD on ONGC E&P capex; AEGISLOG/AEGISVOPAK add LPG/gas terminalling.
themes.driver: Whether the pooled/APM gas-allocation mechanism is restored (the single biggest CGD earnings variable); LNG spot price and Brent; GRM/distillate cracks; ONGC rig tenders & day-rates.

hero.oneLiner: The CrudeChem acquisition has stopped being an integration story and become the company: total income tripled to ₹386.72cr (+165% YoY), oil & gas is now **65% of revenue** (~₹250cr) against a flat-to-slightly-down textile base (₹132cr vs ₹137cr), and consolidated EBITDA margin has climbed back from a post-deal trough of ~14% to **15.70%** as US operating efficiency, supplier renegotiation and green-chemistry mix all landed together. Texas capacity was nearly doubled to 148,000 MTPA during the quarter and is already running at 63% on a **single shift** — so management's USD 100mn (FY27) / USD 200mn (FY28) oil & gas revenue guide needs almost no further capital, only USD 1-2mn for a second shift. The risk is that the whole thesis now rests on one 53%-owned US subsidiary in a cyclical end-market, with no order book in the conventional sense.
